notes.definition: During exercise the body reacts to the increased demand for energy: heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood. If not enough oxygen is supplied, muscles respire anaerobically and lactic acid builds up.
explanation: When you exercise, your muscles contract more often and more strongly, so they need much more energy. This energy comes from respiration, so the muscle cells need a faster supply of glucose and oxygen, and the extra carbon dioxide they produce has to be removed more quickly.

The body responds in three main ways. Heart rate increases, so blood is pumped around the body faster. Breathing rate increases (more breaths per minute) and breath volume increases (more air taken in with each breath). Together these changes supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood, and also carry glucose to the muscles and remove carbon dioxide from them.

During vigorous exercise, the heart and lungs may not be able to supply oxygen fast enough. The muscle cells then respire anaerobically as well as aerobically: glucose → lactic acid. The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so less energy is transferred and lactic acid builds up in the muscles.
During long periods of vigorous activity, muscles become fatigued. Muscle fatigue means the muscles get tired and stop contracting efficiently. This is why you cannot keep up a sprint for very long.

Higher tier: the build-up of lactic acid creates an oxygen debt. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells. Blood flowing through the muscles carries the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. This is why you keep breathing hard and your heart rate stays high for a while after you stop exercising.
keyFacts: Exercise increases the demand for energy, so muscle cells respire faster.
Heart rate increases to pump more oxygenated blood to the muscles.
Breathing rate and breath volume increase to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide.
If too little oxygen reaches the muscles, they respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid.
Anaerobic respiration involves incomplete oxidation of glucose, so lactic acid builds up.
Muscle fatigue: during long periods of vigorous activity, muscles stop contracting efficiently.
Higher: oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with lactic acid and remove it from cells.
Higher: blood carries lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.
Heart rate can be measured by counting the pulse at the wrist or neck.

keyTerms.definition: The number of times the heart beats per minute (bpm).
The number of breaths taken per minute.
The volume of air breathed in (or out) in one breath.
The product of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells; it builds up during vigorous exercise.
When muscles become tired and stop contracting efficiently after long periods of vigorous activity.
(Higher) The amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
The time it takes for heart rate (or breathing rate) to return to its resting value after exercise.

equations.name: Volume of air breathed per minute
equations.formula: volume per minute = breathing rate × breath volume

workedExamples.title: Measuring heart rate
workedExamples.question: A student counts 21 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate her heart rate in beats per minute.
steps: There are 60 seconds in a minute, and 60 ÷ 15 = 4.
Check: 84 beats per minute ÷ 4 = 21 beats in 15 seconds.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change in heart rate
workedExamples.question: A boy's resting heart rate is 65 bpm. During exercise it rises to 156 bpm. Calculate the percentage increase.

workedExamples.title: Volume of air breathed per minute
workedExamples.question: At rest a man takes 12 breaths per minute with a breath volume of 0.5 dm³. During exercise he takes 30 breaths per minute with a breath volume of 2.0 dm³. How many times more air does he breathe per minute during exercise?

workedExamples.title: Calculating an oxygen debt (Higher)
workedExamples.question: After exercise, a runner's oxygen uptake stayed above her resting level by a mean of 0.8 dm³ per minute for 6 minutes. Calculate her oxygen debt.
steps: The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen taken in above resting level after exercise.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think muscles switch completely from aerobic to anaerobic respiration during exercise.
misconceptions.right: In fact aerobic respiration continues; anaerobic respiration happens in addition when the oxygen supply cannot meet the demand.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think heart rate increases to give muscles more blood 'to make energy'.
misconceptions.right: In fact heart rate increases so that more oxygen and glucose reach the muscles for respiration (which transfers energy), and carbon dioxide is removed faster.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think breathing faster is the only change in breathing.
misconceptions.right: In fact both breathing rate AND breath volume (depth of each breath) increase during exercise.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think lactic acid just disappears when you rest.
misconceptions.right: In fact (Higher) blood carries lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. This needs extra oxygen, which is the oxygen debt.

realWorld: Athletes measure how quickly their heart rate returns to normal after exercise (recovery time) to track how their fitness is improving.
Sprinters run short races mostly using anaerobic respiration, so they finish breathing very hard to repay the oxygen debt, while marathon runners pace themselves to stay mainly aerobic.
Fitness watches use heart rate data during training so people can exercise at an intensity that suits their goals.
higherTier: Blood flowing through the muscles transports lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.
Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
This is why heart rate and breathing rate stay high for a time after exercise has stopped.
examTips: When explaining why heart rate increases, link it to oxygen: 'to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood for faster respiration'. Mentioning glucose and carbon dioxide removal adds detail.
Remember all three changes: heart rate, breathing rate AND breath volume. Many students forget breath volume.
Higher: learn the definition of oxygen debt word for word, including 'to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells'.
When reading data from graphs, quote values with units (for example 'rose from 70 bpm to 160 bpm') and calculate changes if asked.
To find heart rate from a 15 second count, multiply by 4; from a 30 second count, multiply by 2.
summary: Exercise increases the demand for energy, so muscles respire faster.
Heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase to supply more oxygenated blood.
If oxygen is short, muscles respire anaerobically and lactic acid builds up.
Long periods of vigorous activity cause muscle fatigue: muscles stop contracting efficiently.
Higher: lactic acid is taken by the blood to the liver and converted back into glucose.
Higher: oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with the lactic acid.

questions.question: What happens to a person's heart rate during exercise?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It stops changing once exercise starts
markScheme: 1 mark: it increases
questions.explanation: The heart beats faster to pump more blood, carrying more oxygen and glucose to the working muscles.

questions.question: Why does breathing rate increase during exercise?
options: To take in more oxygen for respiration
To take in more carbon dioxide
To cool the lungs down
To remove lactic acid through the lungs
markScheme: 1 mark: to take in more oxygen for respiration
questions.explanation: Muscles respire faster, so more oxygen is needed and more carbon dioxide must be removed. We breathe out carbon dioxide, not take it in, and lactic acid is not removed by the lungs.

questions.question: Which substance builds up in muscles during vigorous exercise when there is not enough oxygen?
options: Glucose
Ethanol
Lactic acid
Oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: lactic acid
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration in muscle cells produces lactic acid. Ethanol is made by anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells, not in human muscles.

questions.question: What is the main reason heart rate increases during exercise?
options: To raise blood pressure so the muscles grow
To supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood
To carry lactic acid to the lungs
To cool the body down
markScheme: 1 mark: to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood
questions.explanation: Muscles need more oxygen (and glucose) for faster respiration, so blood must reach them faster. Lactic acid is carried to the liver, not the lungs.

questions.question: What is meant by muscle fatigue?
options: Muscles grow larger after exercise
Muscles stop respiring completely
Muscles get tired and stop contracting efficiently
Muscles respire aerobically only
markScheme: 1 mark: muscles get tired and stop contracting efficiently
questions.explanation: During long periods of vigorous activity, muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently. They do not stop respiring completely; living cells always respire.

questions.question: After exercise, where is lactic acid carried by the blood?
options: To the lungs
To the kidneys
To the heart
To the liver
markScheme: 1 mark: to the liver
questions.explanation: Blood flowing through the muscles carries lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.

questions.question: What is lactic acid converted into in the liver?
options: Glucose
Urea
Ethanol
Carbon dioxide only
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose
questions.explanation: The liver converts lactic acid back into glucose. Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids, which is a different process.

questions.question: Which is the best definition of oxygen debt?
options: The oxygen used by muscles during exercise
The amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells
The difference between the oxygen breathed in and breathed out at rest
The oxygen that muscles store for use during exercise
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells
questions.explanation: Oxygen debt is about the extra oxygen needed AFTER exercise to deal with lactic acid. Muscles do not store oxygen in this way, and oxygen used during exercise is not the debt.

questions.question: What is meant by the term breath volume?
options: The number of breaths taken per minute
The total volume of the lungs
The volume of air breathed in or out in one breath
The volume of oxygen in the blood
markScheme: 1 mark: the volume of air breathed in or out in one breath
questions.explanation: Breath volume is about each single breath. The number of breaths per minute is breathing rate. Both increase during exercise.

questions.question: A runner stops running but continues to breathe deeply and quickly for several minutes. What is the main reason?
options: To take in extra oxygen to react with the lactic acid that has built up
To breathe out the lactic acid
Because the muscles are still contracting hard
To cool the blood in the lungs
markScheme: 1 mark: to take in extra oxygen to react with the lactic acid that has built up
questions.explanation: This is repaying the oxygen debt. Extra oxygen is needed to deal with the accumulated lactic acid. Lactic acid is not breathed out, and the muscles are no longer working hard.

questions.question: Why does lactic acid build up in muscles during vigorous exercise?
options: Too much oxygen reaches the muscles
Glucose is completely oxidised
The liver makes lactic acid and sends it to the muscles
The oxidation of glucose is incomplete because there is not enough oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: the oxidation of glucose is incomplete because there is not enough oxygen
questions.explanation: When the oxygen supply cannot keep up, muscles respire anaerobically. Glucose is only partly oxidised, forming lactic acid. Complete oxidation would form carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question:
Two people did the same exercise.
Table 1 shows how long it took for each person's heart rate to return to its resting value after the exercise.
Which conclusion is best supported by the data in Table 1?

headers: Time for heart rate to return to resting value in minutes

options: Person A is probably fitter than Person B
Person B is probably fitter than Person A
Person A did more exercise than Person B
Person B has a lower resting heart rate
markScheme: 1 mark: Person A is probably fitter than Person B
questions.explanation: A shorter recovery time usually indicates a fitter person. The exercise was the same, so A did not do more. The data says nothing about resting heart rates.

questions.question: State three changes that happen in the body during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: heart rate increases
1 mark: breathing rate increases
1 mark: breath volume increases
questions.explanation: These three changes work together: more air into the lungs per minute, and faster blood flow to carry the oxygen to the muscles.

questions.question: Explain why a person's heart rate increases during exercise.
markScheme: 1 mark: to pump more (oxygenated) blood to the muscles / deliver more oxygen and glucose
1 mark: for faster (aerobic) respiration to transfer more energy for contraction / to remove carbon dioxide faster
questions.explanation: The muscles need more energy, which comes from respiration. Respiration needs oxygen and glucose, which are delivered by the blood.

questions.question: Explain why lactic acid builds up in muscles during a sprint.
markScheme: 1 mark: not enough oxygen reaches the muscles, so they respire anaerobically
1 mark: incomplete oxidation of glucose produces lactic acid
questions.explanation: In a sprint the demand for energy is very high. The heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen fast enough, so anaerobic respiration adds energy, producing lactic acid.

questions.question: Describe what happens to muscles during long periods of vigorous activity.
markScheme: 1 mark: they become fatigued / stop contracting efficiently
questions.explanation: This is muscle fatigue. The muscles can still contract, but not efficiently.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the lactic acid in a person's muscles after they finish exercising.
markScheme: 1 mark: blood flowing through the muscles carries lactic acid away
1 mark: to the liver
1 mark: where it is converted back into glucose (using extra oxygen / the oxygen debt)
questions.explanation: This is how the oxygen debt is repaid. Extra oxygen is needed to react with the lactic acid and remove it from cells.

questions.question: Define the term oxygen debt.
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of extra oxygen needed after exercise
1 mark: to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: what it is (extra oxygen after exercise) and what it is for (dealing with lactic acid).

questions.question: Describe how a student could measure their heart rate in beats per minute.
markScheme: 1 mark: find the pulse at the wrist or neck (using two fingers, not the thumb)
1 mark: count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 / count for 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Heart rate is beats per minute, so a shorter count must be scaled up. A fitness monitor or heart rate monitor can also be used.

questions.question: Suggest why a trained athlete can run for longer than an untrained person before their muscles become fatigued.
markScheme: 1 mark: the athlete's heart and lungs can supply more oxygen to the muscles
1 mark: so less anaerobic respiration happens / less lactic acid builds up
questions.explanation: Training improves oxygen delivery, so the muscles can keep respiring aerobically at higher work rates. Less lactic acid means fatigue sets in later.

questions.question:
A student counted 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds.
Calculate the student's heart rate in beats per minute.
markScheme: 1 mark: 18 × 4 = 72 bpm
questions.explanation: 15 seconds is a quarter of a minute, so multiply by 4: 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a girl's heart rate at rest and during exercise.
Calculate the percentage increase in her heart rate.

headers: Heart rate in beats per minute

markScheme: 1 mark: 120%
questions.explanation: Increase = 154 − 70 = 84 bpm. 84 ÷ 70 × 100 = 120%. Dividing by 154 instead of the original value gives 54.5%, which is wrong.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a man's breathing at rest.
Use the equation:
volume of air breathed per minute = breathing rate × breath volume
Calculate the volume of air he breathes per minute at rest.

headers: Breathing rate in breaths per minute

questions.answerLabel: Volume of air breathed per minute
markScheme: 1 mark: 7.5 dm³/min
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of breaths per minute by the volume of each breath: 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 dm³ per minute.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a man's breathing at rest and during hard exercise.
Use the equation:
volume of air breathed per minute = breathing rate × breath volume
Calculate how many times more air he breathes per minute during exercise than at rest.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

headers: Breathing rate in breaths per minute

markScheme: 1 mark: at rest 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 dm³/min
1 mark: during exercise 40 × 2.5 = 100 dm³/min
questions.explanation: Work out each volume per minute first, then divide. 100 ÷ 7.5 = 13.33..., which is 13.3 to 3 significant figures. Comparing only breathing rates (40 ÷ 15 = 2.67) ignores the change in breath volume.

markScheme: 1 mark: exercise ends at 4 minutes and heart rate returns to resting at 9 minutes, so 9 − 4 = 5 minutes
questions.explanation: From Figure 1, exercise stops at 4 minutes and the heart rate is back to its resting value (70 beats per minute) at 9 minutes. Recovery time = 9 − 4 = 5 minutes. Answering 9 minutes counts from the start of the experiment instead.

questions.question:
A man's resting heart rate is 80 beats per minute.
During exercise his heart rate increases by 85%.
Calculate his heart rate during exercise.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 80 × 0.85 = 68 bpm (or 80 × 1.85)
1 mark: 148 bpm
questions.explanation: An 85% increase means the new value is 185% of the original: 80 × 1.85 = 148 bpm. Answering 68 gives only the increase, not the new heart rate.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows an athlete's oxygen uptake at rest and in the 5 minutes after a sprint.
The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen taken in after exercise, above the resting level.
Calculate the size of the athlete's oxygen debt.

headers: Oxygen uptake in dm³ per minute
rows: Mean for the 5 minutes after the sprint

markScheme: 1 mark: 6 dm³
questions.explanation: The extra oxygen taken in each minute above resting is 1.5 − 0.3 = 1.2 dm³. Over 5 minutes the oxygen debt is 1.2 × 5 = 6 dm³. Using 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 dm³ forgets to subtract the resting uptake.

questions.question: Describe and explain the changes that happen in the body during exercise.
markScheme: Indicative content: muscles contract more, so they need more energy; energy comes from respiration, so more oxygen and glucose are needed; heart rate increases to pump more oxygenated blood to muscles; breathing rate and breath volume increase to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide; if oxygen supply is not enough, anaerobic respiration happens; lactic acid builds up; long vigorous activity leads to muscle fatigue (muscles stop contracting efficiently).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes several changes (heart rate, breathing rate, breath volume) and explains them in terms of the demand for oxygen and energy for respiration.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes one or two changes with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Each change should be linked to its purpose. 'Heart rate increases' is a description; 'to deliver more oxygen for respiration' is the explanation that moves you up a level.

questions.question:
An athlete runs a 400 m race as fast as she can.
Figure 1 shows her heart rate before, during and after the race. She also keeps breathing heavily for several minutes after the race.
Explain the changes in her body during and after the race.

markScheme: Indicative content: during the race muscles need much more energy, so respiration increases; heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood and glucose; breathing rate and breath volume increase to take in more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide; oxygen supply cannot meet demand, so muscles also respire anaerobically; incomplete oxidation of glucose produces lactic acid, which builds up; muscles may become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently; this creates an oxygen debt; after the race, heart rate and breathing stay high to supply the extra oxygen; oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from cells; blood carries lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose; heart rate and breathing fall back to resting levels once the debt is repaid.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically linked explanation of changes during and after the race, including anaerobic respiration, lactic acid, oxygen debt and the role of the liver.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains changes during the race with some reference to lactic acid or oxygen debt after the race, but with gaps in linking.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of increased heart rate or breathing with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A top answer tells the full story in order: high energy demand, increased heart and breathing rates, anaerobic respiration and lactic acid, then the oxygen debt being repaid after the race as lactic acid is taken to the liver.
